title: Behavioural nudges increase COVID-19 vaccinations
abstract: Abstract Enhancing vaccine uptake is a critical public health challenge 1 . Overcoming vaccine hesitancy 2,3 and failure to follow through on vaccination intentions 3 requires effective communication strategies 3,4 . Here we present two sequential randomized controlled trials to test the effect of behavioural interventions on the uptake of COVID-19 vaccines. We designed text-based reminders that make vaccination salient and easy, and delivered them to participants drawn from a healthcare system one day (first randomized controlled trial) ( n = 93,354 participants; clinicaltrials number NCT04800965) and eight days (second randomized controlled trial) ( n = 67,092 individuals; clinicaltrials number NCT04801524) after they received a notification of vaccine eligibility. The first reminder boosted appointment and vaccination rates within the healthcare system by 6.07 (84%) and 3.57 (26%) percentage points, respectively; the second reminder increased those outcomes by 1.65 and 1.06 percentage points, respectively. The first reminder had a greater effect when it was designed to make participants feel ownership of the vaccine dose. However, we found no evidence that combining the first reminder with a video-based information intervention designed to address vaccine hesitancy heightened its effect. We performed online studies ( n = 3,181 participants) to examine vaccination intentions, which revealed patterns that diverged from those of the first randomized controlled trial; this underscores the importance of pilot-testing interventions in the field. Our findings inform the design of behavioural nudges for promoting health decisions 5 , and highlight the value of making vaccination easy and inducing feelings of ownership over vaccines.

claims.text: In the first RCT, receiving a text reminder boosted first-dose appointment rates within UCLA Health by 6.07 percentage points (an 84% relative increase) within six days.
In the first RCT, receiving a text reminder boosted vaccination rates within UCLA Health by 3.57 percentage points (a 26% relative increase) within four weeks.
In the second RCT, receiving a second text reminder increased appointment rates within UCLA Health by 1.65 percentage points within six days.
In the second RCT, receiving a second text reminder increased vaccination rates within UCLA Health by 1.06 percentage points within four weeks.
Adding psychological ownership language to the first reminder increased appointment rates at UCLA Health by 1.51 percentage points compared to reminders without ownership language.
Adding psychological ownership language to the first reminder increased vaccination rates at UCLA Health by 1.09 percentage points compared to reminders without ownership language.

Combining the first text reminder with a video-based information intervention produced no statistically significant evidence of an improvement in appointment or vaccination rates relative to reminders without a video.
In the first RCT, text reminders increased vaccinations obtained anywhere (inside or outside UCLA Health) by 2.1 percentage points within four weeks.
In the first RCT, the reminder effect on appointments was 4.4 percentage points larger among participants who received an influenza shot in recent seasons compared to those who did not.

In online experiments, the video intervention caused a small, statistically significant increase in self-reported interest in getting the vaccine, whereas ownership language produced no evidence of increasing vaccination intentions.

limitations.text: The RCT patient sample consists of predominantly elderly and white participants and is not representative of broader populations.
Less than 21% of the participants in the first RCT opted to watch the linked 2-minute educational video.
The effect of receiving a second text reminder on vaccination rates anywhere was not statistically significant at four weeks (P = 0.127).
Reminders were designed to remove barriers specifically at UCLA Health rather than at a broad set of vaccination locations.
Surveys of vaccination intentions do not always reflect real behaviours, yielding discrepancies when compared with actual field uptake.

future_work.text: Investigating when and under what conditions information interventions can successfully overcome vaccine hesitancy.
Evaluating behavioral nudge messaging designs aimed at motivating health-related behaviors more broadly, such as scheduling preventive care tests or health program participation.

methodologies.name: Sequential randomized controlled trials (RCTs)
methodologies.description: Two sequential large-scale field RCTs were conducted via SMS to test behavioural interventions on COVID-19 vaccine appointment scheduling and uptake at 1 day and 8 days post-eligibility invitation.
datasets: UCLA Health primary and specialty care attributed patient records
conditions: First RCT: Holdout vs Follow-through reminder (2x2 factorial: Basic vs Ownership framing x Link vs No link to 2-minute informational video)
Second RCT: Holdout vs Follow-through reminder (2x3 factorial: Prosocial vs Personal messaging x Early access framing vs Fresh start framing vs Standard)

methodologies.name: Preregistered online experiments on vaccination intentions
methodologies.description: Three randomized online experiments evaluating hypothetical appointment scheduling likelihood, persuasiveness, and vaccination interest in response to reminder interventions.
